stimuli.title: Seven persons in a row facing south
stimuli.content:
Seven persons Aman, Bhoomi, Chirayu, Dhara, Eklavya, Gunjan and Hitesh sit in a straight row, all facing south. (For a person facing south, the right is towards the west and the left is towards the east.)

- Hitesh sits at one of the extreme ends of the row.
- Only two persons sit between Hitesh and Aman.
- Gunjan sits immediately to the right of Aman.
- Dhara sits third to the left of Gunjan.
- Chirayu is an immediate neighbour of Hitesh.
- Bhoomi sits immediately to the left of Aman.
stimuli.solution:
Hitesh is at an end and Aman is three seats from him. Gunjan is immediately to Aman's right (west) and Dhara third to Gunjan's left (east), so Dhara is two seats east of Aman. If Hitesh were at the east end (seat 7 from the west), Aman = 4, Gunjan = 3 and Dhara = 6, and Chirayu, Hitesh's neighbour, would need seat 6: rejected. So Hitesh is at the west end (seat 1), Aman = 4, Gunjan = 3, Dhara = 6, Chirayu = 2, Bhoomi (immediately to Aman's left, i.e. east) = 5 and Eklavya = 7.

| Seat (west to east) | Person |
|---|---|
| 1 | Hitesh |
| 2 | Chirayu |
| 3 | Gunjan |
| 4 | Aman |
| 5 | Bhoomi |
| 6 | Dhara |
| 7 | Eklavya |

stimuli.title: Six persons in a row of nine seats
stimuli.content:
A row has nine seats, numbered 1 to 9 from the left end. Six persons Jignesh, Kritika, Manan, Nupur, Parth and Rachna sit in six of the seats, all facing north; the other three seats are vacant.

- Kritika sits at the extreme left end of the row.
- Exactly one seat lies between Kritika and Parth, and that seat is vacant.
- Manan sits immediately to the right of Parth.
- Jignesh sits third to the right of Nupur.
- Rachna sits second to the left of Jignesh.
- The seat immediately to the right of Rachna is vacant.
- Neither of the two end seats of the row is vacant.
stimuli.solution:
Kritika = 1, seat 2 is vacant, Parth = 3 and Manan = 4. Rachna is second to the left of Jignesh and Jignesh third to the right of Nupur, so Nupur, Rachna and Jignesh sit at n, n + 1 and n + 3. Seat 9 must be occupied, and only these three persons are left, so Jignesh = 9, Rachna = 7 and Nupur = 6. Seat 8 (to Rachna's right) and seat 5 are vacant.

| Seat | Occupant |
|---|---|
| 1 | Kritika |
| 2 | vacant |
| 3 | Parth |
| 4 | Manan |
| 5 | vacant |
| 6 | Nupur |
| 7 | Rachna |
| 8 | vacant |
| 9 | Jignesh |

stimuli.title: A row of unknown length
stimuli.content:
Some persons sit in a straight row, all facing north. The number of persons in the row is not given. Aarti, Bharat, Chhavi, Dinesh, Eshita, Faisal, Girija and Hemant are among them.

- Dinesh sits sixth from the left end of the row.
- Only two persons sit between Dinesh and Eshita.
- Faisal sits fourth to the left of Eshita.
- Aarti sits second to the left of Faisal.
- Bharat sits third to the right of Eshita.
- As many persons sit between Aarti and Bharat as between Bharat and Hemant.
- Hemant sits at one of the extreme ends of the row.
- Girija sits exactly in the middle of the row.
- Only five persons sit between Girija and Chhavi.
stimuli.solution:
Count positions from the left end. Dinesh = 6, so Eshita = 3 or 9. Faisal is four places to Eshita's left, which is impossible from 3, so Eshita = 9, Faisal = 5, Aarti = 3 and Bharat = 12. Eight persons sit between Aarti and Bharat, so Hemant is nine places from Bharat: 3 (Aarti's seat) or 21. Hence Hemant = 21, and as he is at an end, the row has 21 persons. The middle of 21 is 11 (Girija). Chhavi is six places from Girija: 5 (Faisal's seat) or 17, so Chhavi = 17.

| Position from the left | Person |
|---|---|
| 3 | Aarti |
| 5 | Faisal |
| 6 | Dinesh |
| 9 | Eshita |
| 11 | Girija |
| 12 | Bharat |
| 17 | Chhavi |
| 21 | Hemant |

All other positions are held by persons whose names are not given.

stimuli.title: Two rows facing the same way
stimuli.content:
Ten persons Aditya, Bela, Chetna, Darshan, Esha, Gopal, Indu, Jatin, Kirti and Lalit sit in two parallel rows of five seats each. All of them face north. Row 1 is in front (to the north) and Row 2 is directly behind it, so each person in Row 2 sits directly behind one person of Row 1. Who sits in which row is not given.

- Aditya sits in the middle of one of the rows.
- The person who sits directly in front of Aditya sits immediately to the right of Indu.
- Chetna sits directly behind Kirti.
- Kirti is an immediate neighbour of Darshan.
- Gopal and Bela sit at the two extreme ends of the same row.
- Lalit sits immediately to the right of Chetna.
- Esha sits second to the left of Chetna.
- Jatin does not sit directly behind Gopal.
stimuli.solution:
Someone sits in front of Aditya, so Aditya is in the middle of Row 2, and the person in front of him (Row 1, seat 3) is immediately to the right of Indu: Indu is at Row 1, seat 2. Chetna sits behind Kirti, so Kirti is in Row 1 and Chetna in Row 2. Chetna has Lalit on her right and Esha second to her left, so Chetna is at seat 3 or 4 of Row 2; seat 3 is Aditya's, so Chetna = Row 2 seat 4, Esha = seat 2, Lalit = seat 5, and Kirti = Row 1 seat 4. Darshan is next to Kirti: Row 1 seat 3 or 5. Gopal and Bela must be at both ends of one row; Row 2 already has Lalit at an end, so they take Row 1 seats 1 and 5, which puts Darshan at Row 1 seat 3. Jatin takes Row 2 seat 1; he is not behind Gopal, so Bela = Row 1 seat 1 and Gopal = Row 1 seat 5.

| Seat (west to east) | Row 1 (front) | Row 2 (behind) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Bela | Jatin |
| 2 | Indu | Esha |
| 3 | Darshan | Aditya |
| 4 | Kirti | Chetna |
| 5 | Gopal | Lalit |

stimuli.title: Seven persons and a vacant chair
stimuli.content:
Eight chairs are placed around a circular table, equally spaced. Seven persons Mahi, Nirav, Oshin, Prakash, Qadir, Rupa and Sagar sit on seven of them, all facing the centre; one chair is vacant. Positions such as 'second to the right' are counted by chairs, including the vacant chair.

- Mahi sits opposite Nirav.
- The vacant chair is second to the right of Mahi.
- Sagar sits immediately to the left of Nirav.
- Oshin sits second to the right of Sagar.
- Prakash sits immediately to the left of Mahi.
- Qadir does not sit next to the vacant chair.
stimuli.solution:
Fix Mahi. Nirav is opposite her (four chairs away), the vacant chair is second to her right and Prakash immediately to her left. Sagar is immediately to Nirav's left, i.e. between the vacant chair and Nirav, and Oshin is second to Sagar's right, i.e. immediately to Nirav's right. The two chairs left are the one between Mahi and the vacant chair and the one between Oshin and Prakash. Qadir cannot sit next to the vacant chair, so Qadir sits between Oshin and Prakash and Rupa between Mahi and the vacant chair.

| Chair (anticlockwise from Mahi) | Occupant |
|---|---|
| 0 | Mahi |
| 1 | Rupa |
| 2 | the vacant chair |
| 3 | Sagar |
| 4 | Nirav |
| 5 | Oshin |
| 6 | Qadir |
| 7 | Prakash |

stimuli.title: Seven persons around a circle, facing in or out
stimuli.content:
Seven persons Anirudh, Bindiya, Chandra, Deepak, Eshani, Firdaus and Gagan sit around a circular table, equally spaced. Some of them face the centre and the others face outside. (For a person facing the centre the right is anticlockwise; for a person facing outside the right is clockwise.)

- Anirudh faces the centre, and Chandra sits second to the right of Anirudh.
- Gagan sits between Anirudh and Chandra and faces outside.
- Firdaus is an immediate neighbour of Anirudh.
- Bindiya sits second to the right of Firdaus.
- Deepak sits immediately to the right of Bindiya.
- Chandra sits immediately to the right of Eshani.
- Exactly three persons face outside.
- Deepak and Chandra face the same direction.
stimuli.solution:
Fix Anirudh (facing the centre). Chandra is two seats anticlockwise from him and Gagan (facing outside) sits between them; Firdaus takes the seat on Anirudh's other side. If Firdaus faced the centre, second to his right would be Gagan's seat, so Firdaus faces outside and Bindiya sits two seats clockwise from him. The two seats left lie on either side of Bindiya. Chandra is immediately to Eshani's right, so Eshani is Chandra's neighbour (the seat between Chandra and Bindiya) and, to have Chandra on her right, faces outside. Deepak takes the seat between Bindiya and Firdaus; being immediately to Bindiya's right, he makes Bindiya face the centre. Gagan, Firdaus and Eshani are the three facing outside, so Chandra and Deepak face the centre.

| Anticlockwise from Anirudh | Person | Faces |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | Anirudh | centre |
| 1 | Gagan | outside |
| 2 | Chandra | centre |
| 3 | Eshani | outside |
| 4 | Bindiya | centre |
| 5 | Deepak | centre |
| 6 | Firdaus | outside |

stimuli.title: Two concentric circles
stimuli.content:
Eight persons Harini, Ibrahim, Juhi, Kishore, Leena, Mridul, Nayan and Oindrila sit around two concentric circular tables, four at each, equally spaced. The persons at the inner table face outside, and those at the outer table face the centre, so every inner person faces exactly one outer person. Positions such as 'to the right' are counted among the persons of one's own circle.

- Harini sits in the outer circle and faces Nayan.
- Mridul sits second to the right of Harini.
- Leena faces Mridul.
- Juhi sits immediately to the right of Leena.
- Kishore faces Juhi.
- Ibrahim is an immediate neighbour of Nayan.
stimuli.solution:
Harini is in the outer circle facing Nayan (inner). Facing the centre, Harini's right is anticlockwise, so Mridul is the outer seat opposite Harini, and Leena (inner) faces Mridul. Leena faces outside, so her right is clockwise; the inner seat immediately clockwise of Leena is Juhi's, and Kishore is the outer person facing Juhi, i.e. immediately to Harini's right. Ibrahim must sit beside Nayan in the inner circle; the only free inner seat is the one opposite Juhi, so Ibrahim sits there, and Oindrila takes the last outer seat, facing Ibrahim.

| Place (anticlockwise) | Outer circle (faces centre) | Inner circle (faces outside) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Harini | Nayan |
| 2 | Kishore | Juhi |
| 3 | Mridul | Leena |
| 4 | Oindrila | Ibrahim |

stimuli.title: Nine flats on three floors
stimuli.content:
Nine persons Ankur, Barkha, Charan, Disha, Emon, Falak, Gaurang, Heer and Imtiaz live in a three-storey building, one in each flat. Floor 1 is the lowermost and floor 3 the topmost. Each floor has three flats in a line from west to east: West, Middle and East. Each flat is directly above the flat of the same name on the floor below.

- Imtiaz lives in a Middle flat, but not on the topmost floor.
- Ankur lives in the flat directly above Imtiaz's flat.
- Emon lives in the flat directly below Imtiaz's flat.
- Barkha lives in an East flat on the same floor as Imtiaz.
- Disha lives in the flat directly above Barkha's flat.
- Heer lives in the flat directly above Charan's flat, and both live in West flats.
- Falak lives in a West flat, on the same floor as Gaurang.
stimuli.solution:
Imtiaz has a flat above him (Ankur) and a flat below him (Emon), so Imtiaz must be in 2-Middle, Ankur in 3-Middle and Emon in 1-Middle. Barkha is in 2-East and Disha above her in 3-East. The West flats of all three floors and 1-East are left. Heer is directly above Charan in the West column, so they take 3-West/2-West or 2-West/1-West, and Falak takes the remaining West flat. Falak shares a floor with Gaurang, and the only non-West flat left is 1-East, so Falak = 1-West, Gaurang = 1-East, Charan = 2-West and Heer = 3-West.

| Floor | West | Middle | East |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3 | Heer | Ankur | Disha |
| 2 | Charan | Imtiaz | Barkha |
| 1 | Falak | Emon | Gaurang |

stimuli.title: Six floors and six ages
stimuli.content:
Six persons Jayesh, Kesar, Lohit, Madhu, Nitin and Pranali live on the six floors of a building, one on each floor (floor 1 is the lowermost). Their ages, in years, are 24, 27, 31, 35, 38 and 42, one age each.

- The person aged 42 lives on floor 2.
- Jayesh lives two floors above the person aged 42.
- Pranali lives immediately above Jayesh.
- The youngest person lives immediately below Jayesh.
- Jayesh is older than both the persons living above him.
- Lohit lives on the topmost floor and is older than Pranali.
- Madhu is 11 years younger than Kesar.
- Nitin lives above Madhu.
stimuli.solution:
The 42-year-old is on floor 2, Jayesh on 4, Pranali on 5 and the 24-year-old on 3; Lohit is on 6. So Kesar, Madhu and Nitin share floors 1, 2 and 3, where floor 2 holds age 42 and floor 3 age 24. Ages 11 apart are 24–35, 27–38 and 31–42. Madhu 24 (floor 3) is impossible because Nitin must live above Madhu; Madhu 27 with Kesar 38 is impossible because only floor 1 has an age other than 42 and 24. So Kesar is 42 (floor 2) and Madhu 31 on floor 1, leaving floor 3 (24) for Nitin. Floors 4, 5 and 6 share 27, 35 and 38 with Jayesh older than Lohit and Pranali, and Lohit older than Pranali: Jayesh 38, Lohit 35, Pranali 27.

| Floor | Person | Age |
|---|---|---|
| 6 | Lohit | 35 |
| 5 | Pranali | 27 |
| 4 | Jayesh | 38 |
| 3 | Nitin | 24 |
| 2 | Kesar | 42 |
| 1 | Madhu | 31 |

stimuli.title: Eight persons in ten flats
stimuli.content:
A five-storey building has two flats on each floor: flat A to the west and flat B to the east, with each flat A directly above the flat A of the floor below (and likewise for B). Floor 1 is the lowermost. Eight persons Ritesh, Sneh, Tulika, Umang, Varsha, Wahid, Yashvi and Zoravar live in eight of the flats, one in each; two flats are vacant.

- Tulika lives in flat B of an odd-numbered floor, and flat A of her floor is vacant.
- Ritesh lives directly above Tulika.
- Umang lives on the same floor as Ritesh.
- Yashvi lives directly above Umang.
- The flat directly above Ritesh's flat is vacant.
- Sneh lives in flat B, two floors below Ritesh.
- Varsha lives in flat A on a floor below Zoravar's floor.
- Wahid lives on the lowermost floor.
stimuli.solution:
Tulika is in flat B of floor 1, 3 or 5. Floor 5 leaves no flat above her for Ritesh. Floor 1 puts Ritesh in 2-B, and Sneh would have to live two floors below floor 2: impossible. So Tulika = 3-B (3-A vacant), Ritesh = 4-B, 5-B vacant, Umang = 4-A, Yashvi = 5-A and Sneh = 2-B. That uses both vacant flats, so 1-A, 1-B and 2-A are occupied by Varsha, Wahid and Zoravar. Wahid is on floor 1; Varsha is in a flat A below Zoravar, so Varsha = 1-A, Zoravar = 2-A and Wahid = 1-B.

| Floor | Flat A (west) | Flat B (east) |
|---|---|---|
| 5 | Yashvi | vacant |
| 4 | Umang | Ritesh |
| 3 | vacant | Tulika |
| 2 | Zoravar | Sneh |
| 1 | Varsha | Wahid |

stimuli.title: Six boxes in two stacks
stimuli.content:
Six boxes D, F, H, J, L and N are kept in two stacks, X (on the left) and Y (on the right), with three boxes in each stack. Level 1 is the bottom of a stack and level 3 its top.

- Box J is in stack X.
- Box D is placed directly above box J.
- Box H is at the top of the stack that does not contain box D.
- Box L is at the same level as box D, but in the other stack.
- Box F is placed below box L in the same stack.
- Box N is not at the bottom of either stack.
stimuli.solution:
Box J is in stack X with D directly above it, so J and D are at levels 1–2 or 2–3 of stack X. L sits at D's level in stack Y, and H is at the top of stack Y. If D were at level 3, L would also be at level 3 of Y, which is H's place. So J = X1, D = X2 and L = Y2. F is below L: Y1. N takes the remaining place, X3 (not a bottom place).

| Level | Stack X | Stack Y |
|---|---|---|
| 3 | N | H |
| 2 | D | L |
| 1 | J | F |

stimuli.title: Seven boxes and their weights
stimuli.content:
Seven boxes B, C, E, G, I, K and M are placed one above another in a single stack. Their weights are 10 kg, 14 kg, 17 kg, 21 kg, 25 kg, 28 kg and 32 kg, one weight per box.

- Box G is the heaviest box and is placed third from the bottom.
- Only two boxes are placed between box G and the lightest box.
- Box I is placed immediately above the lightest box and weighs 17 kg.
- Box K is placed at the bottom of the stack and weighs twice as much as box C.
- Box C is placed immediately above box K.
- Box E is placed immediately above box M, and E is heavier than M.
stimuli.solution:
G (32 kg) is third from the bottom, so the lightest box is three places from it: sixth from the bottom. I (17 kg) is seventh. K is at the bottom and C second. Among the weights left (10, 14, 21, 25, 28) the only pair where one is twice the other is 14 and 28, so K = 28 kg and C = 14 kg. E sits immediately above M, so they take places 4 and 5 (if they took 5 and 6, E would be the lightest, yet heavier than M). B takes place 6 and is the lightest (10 kg). E is heavier than M: E = 25, M = 21.

| Place from the bottom | Box | Weight |
|---|---|---|
| 7 | I | 17 kg |
| 6 | B | 10 kg |
| 5 | E | 25 kg |
| 4 | M | 21 kg |
| 3 | G | 32 kg |
| 2 | C | 14 kg |
| 1 | K | 28 kg |

stimuli.title: A stack of unknown size
stimuli.content:
Some boxes are placed one above another in a single stack. The number of boxes is not given. Boxes R, S, T, U, V, W, X and Y are among them; the other boxes are unnamed.

- Box T is placed fifth from the bottom.
- Only three boxes are placed between box T and box W.
- Box V is placed immediately below box W.
- As many boxes are placed above box W as below box T.
- Box R is placed exactly in the middle of the stack.
- Only two boxes are placed between box R and box S, and S is placed above V.
- Only one box is placed between box U and box S, and U is not at the top of the stack.
- Box X is at the top of the stack, and box Y is placed second from the bottom.
stimuli.solution:
Number places from the bottom. T = 5, so W = 9 or 1; V is immediately below W, so W = 9 and V = 8. Four boxes are below T, so four are above W: the stack has 9 + 4 = 13 boxes. R is in the middle, 7th. S is three places from R (4 or 10) and above V (8), so S = 10. U is two places from S (8 or 12); 8 is V's place, so U = 12, which is not the top. X = 13 and Y = 2.

| Place from the bottom | Box |
|---|---|
| 13 | X |
| 12 | U |
| 10 | S |
| 9 | W |
| 8 | V |
| 7 | R |
| 5 | T |
| 2 | Y |

The other places hold unnamed boxes.

stimuli.title: Seven trainings from March to September
stimuli.content:
Seven employees Akhil, Bhargavi, Chetas, Dipti, Ehsan, Firoza and Gautam attend a training programme, one in each month from March to September of the same year.

- Akhil's training is in a month that has 31 days.
- Chetas's training is in a month after Akhil's, and only one person's training is between theirs.
- Firoza's training is in the month immediately before Chetas's.
- Bhargavi's training is in the month immediately after Chetas's.
- Ehsan's training is in a month that has 30 days, after Bhargavi's.
- Gautam's training is in a month that has 30 days.
- Dipti's training is in a month before Gautam's.
stimuli.solution:
Akhil, Firoza, Chetas and Bhargavi take four consecutive months, with Akhil's month having 31 days, and Ehsan comes later in a 30-day month. Akhil in July or August leaves no room. Akhil in March gives Firoza April, Chetas May, Bhargavi June and Ehsan September; Dipti and Gautam would take July and August, but Gautam's month must have 30 days: rejected. So Akhil = May, Firoza = June, Chetas = July, Bhargavi = August, Ehsan = September, and Gautam (30 days, after Dipti) = April, Dipti = March.

stimuli.title: Six visits on six dates of July
stimuli.content:
Six persons Harshad, Ishita, Jairaj, Kalyani, Lavesh and Meghna visit a bank branch on six different dates of July: the 3rd, 8th, 12th, 17th, 23rd and 28th. Each person visits once.

- Ishita visits on an odd-numbered date after the 12th.
- Only one person visits between Ishita and Jairaj.
- Lavesh visits on the date immediately after Ishita's (no one visits between them).
- Harshad visits on an even-numbered date, before Meghna.
- Kalyani visits before Harshad.
- Meghna visits on a date that is a multiple of 4, and before Jairaj.
stimuli.solution:
Ishita visits on the 17th or the 23rd, with Lavesh on the next date of the list. If Ishita = 23rd, Lavesh = 28th and Jairaj = 12th; Meghna must be before Jairaj on a multiple of 4, i.e. the 8th, and Harshad before her on an even date: impossible (only the 3rd is earlier). So Ishita = 17th and Lavesh = 23rd, and Jairaj, two dates away from Ishita, is on the 8th or the 28th. Meghna (a multiple of 4) must come before Jairaj, which rules out the 8th, so Jairaj = 28th. Kalyani, Harshad and Meghna take the 3rd, 8th and 12th in that order (Kalyani before Harshad before Meghna).

| Date (July) | Person |
|---|---|
| 3 | Kalyani |
| 8 | Harshad |
| 12 | Meghna |
| 17 | Ishita |
| 23 | Lavesh |
| 28 | Jairaj |

stimuli.content:
Six friends Neeraj, Ovi, Pramod, Ruchi, Sumit and Tanisha were born in six different months of the same year (not a leap year). In each of the other six months none of them was born.

- Neeraj was born in a month that has 30 days.
- Tanisha was born in the month immediately after Neeraj's month.
- Pramod was born after Tanisha, and exactly two months lie between their months.
- Ovi was born after Pramod, and exactly one month lies between their months.
- Sumit was born in a month that has 31 days, after Ovi's month.
- Ruchi was born in the shortest month of the year.
stimuli.solution:
Neeraj's month has 30 days: April, June, September or November. Tanisha is the next month, Pramod three months after Tanisha and Ovi two months after Pramod. From September or November the chain runs past December. From June: Tanisha July, Pramod October, Ovi December, and Sumit (31 days, after Ovi) has no month left. So Neeraj = April, Tanisha = May, Pramod = August, Ovi = October and Sumit = December (the only 31-day month after October). Ruchi = February.

|---|---|

stimuli.title: Six officers and their joining years
stimuli.content:
Six officers Vasudha, Waqar, Yamuna, Zeeshan, Aniket and Bhumika joined a bank in six different years among 2013, 2015, 2018, 2019, 2022 and 2024. Each works in a different department among Audit, Credit, HR, IT, Retail and Treasury.

- Vasudha joined in an even-numbered year and works in Credit.
- The person who works in HR joined exactly one year after Vasudha.
- Zeeshan works in HR.
- Aniket joined exactly nine years after Bhumika.
- The person who works in Treasury joined most recently.
- Yamuna joined after Zeeshan but before Aniket.
- The person who works in Audit joined earliest.
- Bhumika does not work in Retail.
stimuli.solution:
The only two listed years one year apart are 2018 and 2019, so Vasudha (even year, Credit) joined in 2018 and Zeeshan (HR) in 2019. Nine-year gaps: 2013–2022 and 2015–2024. If Bhumika = 2013 and Aniket = 2022, Yamuna must join after 2019 and before 2022, which no listed year allows. So Bhumika = 2015, Aniket = 2024 (Treasury, the latest year), Yamuna = 2022 and Waqar = 2013 (Audit, the earliest). IT and Retail remain for Bhumika and Yamuna; Bhumika is not in Retail, so Bhumika = IT and Yamuna = Retail.

|---|---|---|

| 2015 | Bhumika | IT |

stimuli.title: The return of millets
stimuli.content:
Not long ago, millets such as ragi, jowar and bajra were dismissed in many Indian homes as 'poor man's food'. Rice and wheat, supported by assured government procurement and subsidised distribution, gradually took their place on the plate, and the area under millets shrank steadily over several decades. Today, however, these hardy grains are enjoying a revival, and the reasons are as much about health and climate as about taste.

Nutritionists point out that millets are rich in fibre, iron and calcium, and that they release sugar into the blood more slowly than polished rice. For a country with a rising number of people living with diabetes, this matters a great deal. Farmers, for their part, value millets because they grow on poor soils and need far less water than paddy. In regions where the monsoon is becoming less predictable, a crop that survives a dry spell can be the difference between a modest income and none at all.

The revival has not been easy, though. Millets are harder to process than rice or wheat; the small grains must be cleaned, de-husked and sometimes soaked before they can be cooked, and many villages lack the machines to do this. City consumers who are willing to pay more for millet biscuits and breakfast cereals often have little idea how to cook the grain itself. As a result, a large share of the price paid in a supermarket goes to processors and brands rather than to the farmer.

If the revival is to last, it will need more than enthusiasm. Small processing units close to the farms, fair procurement prices and recipes that suit modern kitchens could together turn a passing trend into a lasting change in what the country grows and eats. The humble millet, in short, deserves to be treated not as a fashion but as a foundation.

stimuli.title: The library that listened
stimuli.content:
For years, the district library in a small town in central India was a quiet, dusty building visited mainly by retired men reading the morning newspapers. Its shelves held old textbooks, its fans rarely worked, and its timings, ten in the morning to five in the evening, suited almost no one who had a job or attended college. Many residents assumed it would simply close one day without anyone noticing.

That changed when a new librarian decided to ask people what they actually wanted. The answers surprised her. Students preparing for competitive examinations wanted a quiet place to study and access to recent guidebooks they could not afford to buy. Young mothers wanted a corner where their children could read picture books. Daily-wage workers wanted help filling in online forms for government schemes. None of them had ever been asked before.

With a modest grant from the municipality and donations from local shops, the library extended its hours into the evening, set up a reading room for aspirants and installed four computers with an internet connection. Volunteers, many of them former students, offered to help visitors with forms and applications. Within two years, daily footfall rose from about thirty to more than four hundred, and a waiting list formed for seats in the reading room.

The story is not unique. Across the country, libraries that were once written off are finding new life by becoming community spaces rather than mere storehouses of books. Their success suggests a simple lesson that applies well beyond libraries: public institutions decline not only when they lack money but when they stop listening to the people they are meant to serve.

stimuli.title: Keeping it fresh
stimuli.content:
India is among the world's largest producers of fruits and vegetables, yet a significant share of what its farmers grow never reaches a consumer. Tomatoes split in the back of overloaded trucks, bananas ripen too early in hot warehouses, and leafy vegetables wilt while waiting for a buyer at a crowded market yard. Estimates of post-harvest loss vary, but even conservative figures suggest that the value lost every year is enormous.

The missing link is the cold chain: the unbroken sequence of pre-cooling, refrigerated storage and refrigerated transport that keeps perishable produce fresh from the farm gate to the retail shelf. A chain, as the name suggests, is only as useful as its weakest link. A cold store in a city is of little help if the produce has already spent eight hours in the sun on its way there. Much of the existing cold storage capacity, moreover, is concentrated in a few states and built for a single crop, the potato, which leaves growers of other perishables with few options.

Building more warehouses is therefore not the whole answer. What farmers need most is small pre-cooling and storage units close to where crops are harvested, along with refrigerated vehicles that can carry produce to distant markets. Such units are expensive to run on unreliable grid power, which is why solar-powered cold rooms that can be shared by a village have attracted attention. Farmer producer organisations, which pool the output of many small growers, are better placed than individual farmers to fill such facilities and to bargain with buyers.

Storage alone, however, does not guarantee a better price. A farmer who can hold back his tomatoes for two weeks gains only if he knows where and when prices will rise, and has the means to reach that market. Information, finance and logistics must therefore advance together. When they do, a cold chain does more than prevent waste: it gives the grower the one thing he has rarely had, the freedom to choose when to sell.

stimuli.title: The missing middle
stimuli.content:
India's health financing has long had an odd shape. The poorest households are covered, at least on paper, by government-funded insurance schemes, while salaried employees in the formal sector usually receive a policy from their employer. Between these two groups lies a large population of shopkeepers, small traders, self-employed professionals and informal workers who are too well-off to qualify for free schemes but not well-off enough to feel that they can afford private cover. Policy researchers call them the 'missing middle'.

For these households, a single hospital admission can wipe out years of savings. Yet many of them do not buy insurance even when a suitable policy is available at a modest premium. The reasons are partly financial and partly psychological. A premium is a certain cost paid today, while an illness is an uncertain event that may never happen, and people tend to give more weight to the first than to the second. Some also see an unused policy as money wasted, much as one might regret buying an umbrella in a year without rain. Others simply distrust insurers, having heard stories of claims rejected on technical grounds.

Insurers have responded with cheaper products, shorter forms and cashless treatment at network hospitals, but take-up has risen only slowly. Experience from other countries suggests that what works best is a combination of measures: making enrolment simple, perhaps through a bank account or a mobile app; pooling small buyers into groups so that premiums fall; and settling claims quickly and transparently so that trust can be built over time.

None of these steps is dramatic. Together, however, they address the real obstacle, which is less the price of a policy than the belief that it will be there when needed. A household that has seen a neighbour's claim paid without fuss is far more likely to buy a policy than one that has only seen an advertisement.

stimuli.title: The power of the default
stimuli.content:
Economics textbooks once assumed that people, given the right information, would make the choices that best served their long-term interests. If saving for retirement was sensible, rational workers would save. Decades of evidence have complicated that picture. People procrastinate, are swayed by how options are presented and, above all, tend to stick with whatever happens if they do nothing. This last tendency, the power of the default, has become one of the most studied ideas in public policy.

Consider a pension scheme in which employees must fill in a form to join. Many who intend to enrol never get round to it, not because they have weighed the scheme and rejected it but because the form sits on a desk for months. Reverse the arrangement, so that employees are enrolled automatically unless they choose to opt out, and participation typically rises sharply, even though the scheme itself has not changed in the slightest. Nobody is forced to save; the path of least resistance has merely been redrawn.

Supporters of such 'nudges' argue that they preserve freedom while correcting predictable lapses. Critics are less comfortable. A default, they point out, is never neutral: someone must choose it, and that someone may have interests of their own. A default contribution rate set too low may leave workers falsely reassured that they are saving enough; a default investment fund chosen for the provider's convenience may serve the provider better than the saver. There is also the question of consent. A choice that people make only because they did not notice they were making it is a curious kind of choice.

The sensible conclusion is not to abandon defaults, which are unavoidable in any case, since every form must begin somewhere, but to design them with care and disclose them openly. If inertia is going to decide outcomes for millions of people, those who set the starting point bear a responsibility that is easy to underestimate precisely because it is so quiet.

stimuli.title: A net or a hammock
stimuli.content:
Deposit insurance is one of the quiet foundations of modern banking. By promising that ordinary depositors will get their money back, up to a fixed limit, even if their bank fails, it removes the main reason for a bank run: the fear that those who wait in the queue will be left with nothing. A rumour that might once have emptied a sound bank in an afternoon now does far less damage, because small savers know their deposits are safe.

Yet the same protection creates a subtler problem, which economists call moral hazard. When people are shielded from the consequences of a risk, they tend to take less care to avoid it. An insured depositor has little reason to ask whether her bank lends prudently, and a bank that knows its depositors will not desert it may be tempted to chase high returns through risky loans. The guarantee that prevents panic can thus weaken the discipline that would otherwise keep banks careful.

Policymakers have tried to strike a balance. Coverage is usually capped, so that large depositors, who are better able to monitor a bank, still bear some risk. Banks pay premiums for the insurance, and some systems charge higher premiums to riskier banks, much as a careless driver pays more for motor insurance. Above all, deposit insurance is paired with regulation and supervision: if depositors no longer watch the banks closely, someone else must.

The arrangement is therefore less a single safety net than a bargain. Society agrees to protect small savers from the failure of institutions they cannot be expected to understand; in return, banks accept rules on capital, liquidity and lending that limit their freedom to gamble with insured money. When either side of that bargain weakens, when coverage expands without matching supervision or when supervisors grow complacent, the safety net can quietly turn into a hammock.

stimuli.title: The bicycle comes back
stimuli.content:
In many Indian cities, the bicycle was once the most common way to get to work. Mill workers, clerks and students rode to their (1) ______ every morning, and a bicycle was a prized possession that was passed down from parent to child. As incomes rose, however, the scooter and the car gradually (2) ______ it, and the cycle came to be seen as a sign of poverty rather than of good sense.

Today, as traffic jams grow longer and the air in many cities becomes harder to breathe, planners are taking a fresh look at this simple machine. A bicycle produces no fumes, takes up little road space and costs almost nothing to run. Regular cycling also keeps the rider fit, which is a real (3) ______ at a time when lifestyle diseases are rising.

The main obstacle is safety. Few people are willing to ride alongside speeding buses and trucks, and most roads offer no separate space for cyclists. Where cities have built protected cycle lanes and secure parking, the number of riders has (4) ______ quickly. Some cities have also introduced public bicycle-sharing schemes, under which a cycle can be hired at one station and returned at another for a small fee.

Such schemes work best when they are (5) ______ to bus and metro stations, so that a commuter can ride the first and last kilometre of the journey. The bicycle will not replace the bus or the train, but it can make them far more useful. A city that makes room for cyclists, in short, makes room for everyone.

stimuli.title: Weavers on the web
stimuli.content:
For generations, handloom weavers in India sold their saris and fabrics through middlemen who bought cheaply in the village and sold at a large profit in the city. The weaver, who might spend weeks on a single piece, rarely knew what the final buyer paid for it. Online marketplaces and social media have begun to (1) ______ this pattern. A weaver with a smartphone can now photograph her work, describe how it was made and sell it directly to a customer hundreds of kilometres away.

The benefits can be (2) ______. Weavers who sell directly report earning noticeably more per piece, and some have built a loyal following among buyers who value the story behind each product. Customers, for their part, gain access to genuine handwoven goods instead of cheaper machine-made (3) ______ that are often passed off as handloom.

Selling online, however, brings new demands. Photographs must be clear, descriptions accurate and parcels packed so that delicate fabric is not damaged. Payments, returns and customer queries must be handled promptly, and a single bad review can (4) ______ sales for weeks. Many weavers, especially older ones, find these tasks daunting and continue to depend on intermediaries.

Weavers' cooperatives and a few non-profit groups are trying to meet this need by offering training in photography, digital payments and basic bookkeeping, and by handling packing and dispatch collectively. Their experience suggests that technology works best when it is (5) ______ by support on the ground. A website can open a door, but someone still has to help the weaver walk through it.

stimuli.title: Learning by doing
stimuli.content:
Every year, millions of young Indians finish school or college with a certificate but little idea of how a workplace actually functions. Employers, in turn, complain that graduates lack practical skills and must be trained almost from scratch. Apprenticeships, in which a young person learns a trade by working under experienced staff while earning a stipend, offer a way to (1) ______ young people with real experience before they enter the job market.

The idea is old. Carpenters, goldsmiths and tailors have always learned by watching and assisting a master. What is new is the attempt to make apprenticeships a formal (2) ______ to employment across industries, from retail and hospitality to banking and manufacturing. For the apprentice, the arrangement offers income, experience and a credential that employers recognise. For the firm, it offers a chance to train future staff in its own methods and to judge their ability before making a permanent offer.

Yet the numbers remain modest compared with the size of the workforce. Small firms, which employ most workers, often find the paperwork (3) ______ and fear that an apprentice will leave as soon as the training is complete. Some larger firms, meanwhile, have been accused of using apprentices as cheap labour, assigning them routine tasks that teach them little.

Making the system work will require simpler rules, so that a small workshop can take on an apprentice without hiring a consultant, and closer (4) ______ of what apprentices actually learn. Industry bodies can help by designing short, practical courses and by certifying skills in a way that is recognised across firms. An apprenticeship that ends with a certificate no one trusts is little better than a degree no one values. If these conditions are met, apprenticeships could become one of the most (5) ______ routes into work for young people who want to learn by doing.

stimuli.title: Too many visitors
stimuli.content:
Every summer, the roads leading to popular hill towns fill with cars, and towns built for a few thousand residents find themselves hosting many times that number of visitors. Hotels are booked out, water tankers run day and night, and garbage piles up faster than the local body can (1) ______ it. What was once a quiet retreat begins to resemble the crowded city the tourists came to escape.

Tourism is, of course, a vital source of income for these regions, where farming is difficult and industry scarce. The problem is not tourism itself but its (2) ______: too many visitors arriving in the same few weeks, staying in the same few places and making demands that fragile mountain slopes cannot bear. Unplanned construction of hotels on steep slopes has made some towns more (3) ______ to landslides, and the loss of forest cover has worsened the damage caused by heavy rain.

Some local governments have begun to experiment with limits. A few have introduced permits for vehicles entering ecologically sensitive areas, while others charge a small green fee whose proceeds are spent on waste management. Promoting lesser-known destinations and off-season travel can also spread visitors more evenly through the year.

Such measures are rarely popular at first. Hotel owners worry about losing business, and visitors resent paying for what was once free. But the alternative is a slow decline in which the very beauty that draws tourists is (4) ______ by their numbers. A hill town that protects its forests, water and slopes is not turning tourists away; it is making sure there will still be something worth visiting in twenty years.

stimuli.title: What your deposit really earns
stimuli.content:
For millions of households, a fixed deposit is the simplest way to save. The interest rate printed on the deposit receipt, however, can be **(1) misleading**. What matters to a saver is not the nominal rate but the real rate: the return left after inflation has been taken into account. If a deposit earns seven per cent a year while prices rise by six per cent, the saver's purchasing power grows by only about one per cent, and if inflation **(2) falls** above the deposit rate, the saver is in effect becoming poorer every year even as the balance on paper keeps rising.

This distinction matters most for those who depend on interest income, such as retired people. When inflation is high and deposit rates lag behind, they face an uncomfortable choice: accept a **(3) gain** in their real income or move their savings into riskier assets in search of higher returns. Many choose the second path without fully understanding the risks, which is one reason why the mis-selling of complex products tends to rise when real rates are **(4) generous**.

Tax adds another layer. Interest on deposits is generally taxed as income, so the post-tax real return can be lower still, or even negative for savers in higher tax brackets. A saver who looks only at the headline rate may therefore greatly overestimate how much her money is really earning.

None of this means that deposits are a poor choice; they remain safe, liquid and easy to understand. It does mean that savers should judge them by the right yardstick. The question to ask is not 'How much interest will I get?' but 'How much more will my money be able to buy at the end of the year?'

solution.concept: BODMAS: both divisions and the multiplication come before the addition and subtraction
solution.explanation: Do the divisions and the multiplication first: 156 ÷ 12 = 13, 7 × 8 = 56 and 45 ÷ 9 = 5. Then 13 + 56 − 5 = 64.
solution.why_others_wrong: 74 adds the 5 instead of subtracting it; 155 adds 13 + 7 before multiplying by 8; 69 drops the last term.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the value of 0.25 × 4.8 + 2⅝ ÷ 0.75 − 1.6?

solution.concept: Convert mixed numbers and decimals to fractions; divide and multiply before adding and subtracting
solution.shortcut: Dividing by 0.75 is multiplying by 4/3: 2.625 × 4/3 = 3.5.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.57 multiplies 2⅝ by 0.75 instead of dividing (1.2 + 1.97 − 1.6 ≈ 1.57); 6.3 adds the 1.6; 2.3 is 3.5 − 1.2, which drops the last term and subtracts the first.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Find the value of √5184 ÷ ∛1728 × √2.25 + 3².

solution.concept: Square roots and cube roots of perfect powers, then left-to-right ÷ and ×
solution.shortcut: 5184 ends in 4 and lies between 70² = 4900 and 75² = 5625, so its root is 72.
solution.why_others_wrong: 13 divides 6 by 1.5 instead of multiplying; 99 takes √2.25 as 15; 15 leaves out the × 1.5.

solution.concept: Negative fractional exponents: a^(−m/n) = 1 ÷ (n-th root of a)^m; write each decimal as a power of a simple fraction
solution.shortcut: A negative exponent flips the base: 0.2 → 5 and 0.5 → 2, then take the powers 5², 2³ and 2¹.
solution.why_others_wrong: 50 divides by 4 instead of 2; 200 multiplies by 2 instead of dividing; 400 multiplies 25 × 8 × 2.

solution.concept: Open brackets from the innermost: ( ), then { }, then [ ]; division comes before subtraction
solution.why_others_wrong: 10.25 divides (45 − 4) by 4; 42.25 works out (15 − 8 + 3) × 2 = 20 inside the round bracket; 41 forgets the ÷ 4.

solution.concept: 'of' is worked out before division (the O in BODMAS)
solution.explanation: The bracket is 2⅖ + 3⅗ = 6. '⅗ of 15' = 9 is evaluated before the division, so 6 ÷ 9 = ⅔. Then ⅔ + 1⅓ = 2.
solution.why_others_wrong: 151⅓ divides by ⅗ first and then multiplies by 15, ignoring that 'of' comes first; 11⅓ drops the 'of 15'; ⅔ forgets to add 1⅓.

solution.concept: Square root of a decimal: the root has half as many decimal places
solution.explanation: √0.000441 = 0.021 (six decimal places become three), √0.0196 = 0.14 and √1.44 = 1.2. Multiplication first: 0.14 × 1.2 = 0.168. Then 0.021 + 0.168 = 0.189.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.378 takes √0.000441 as 0.21; 1.701 takes √0.0196 as 1.4; 0.1932 adds before multiplying.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If x = 3 + 2√2, what is the value of x³ + 1/x³?

solution.concept: Rationalising 1/x, then the identity a³ + b³ = (a + b)³ − 3ab(a + b) with ab = 1
solution.shortcut: Whenever x × (1/x) = 1, x³ + 1/x³ = k³ − 3k with k = x + 1/x.
solution.why_others_wrong: 216 is (x + 1/x)³ without the correction term; 234 adds 3(x + 1/x) instead of subtracting it; 34 is x² + 1/x² = 6² − 2, not the cube expression.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If 2^(x + 3) + 2^(x + 1) = 320, what is the value of x?

solution.concept: Take the lowest power out as a common factor
solution.explanation: 2^(x + 3) = 8 × 2^x and 2^(x + 1) = 2 × 2^x, so the left side is 10 × 2^x. Then 10 × 2^x = 320 gives 2^x = 32 = 2⁵, so x = 5.
solution.why_others_wrong: 6 is the value of x + 1 (factorising as 2^(x + 1)(2² + 1) = 320 gives 2^(x + 1) = 64), not of x; 4 and 3 fail the check: 2⁷ + 2⁵ = 160 and 2⁶ + 2⁴ = 80.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Express 0.2333… (3 recurring) + 0.363636… (36 recurring) as a fraction in its lowest terms.

solution.concept: Converting recurring decimals: pure recurring 0.abab… = ab/99; mixed recurring 0.abbb… = (ab − a)/90
solution.why_others_wrong: 59/99 treats both as pure recurring (23/99 + 36/99); 59/90 treats both as mixed with denominator 90; 19/30 writes 0.3636… as 36/90.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?)?
?² + 15% of 640 − √1296 × 2.5 = 1030 (? is a positive number)

solution.concept: Evaluate every known term, then isolate ?²
solution.why_others_wrong: 30, 34 and 36 give ?² = 900, 1,156 and 1,296, none of which satisfies ?² + 6 = 1030.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Find the value of √(41 − √(21 + √(19 − √9))).

solution.concept: Nested radicals are opened from the innermost root outwards
solution.why_others_wrong: 5 is √25, the value one level inside, not the final root.

solution.concept: Rationalising: 1/(√a − √b) = (√a + √b)/(a − b), and here every a − b = 1
solution.explanation: Each term rationalises to a sum: 1/(√9 − √8) = 3 + √8, 1/(√8 − √7) = √8 + √7, and so on. With the alternating signs, (3 + √8) − (√8 + √7) + (√7 + √6) − (√6 + √5) + (√5 + 2) = 3 + 2 = 5, since all the surds cancel.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0 assumes everything cancels, including 3 and 2; 1 subtracts 2 from 3; 3 + 2√2 keeps only the first term.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should come in place of the question mark (?)?
35.04% of 799.7 − 12.02% of 249.9 ≈ ?

solution.concept: Round each percentage and number to the nearest convenient value
solution.shortcut: 1% of 800 is 8, so 35% is 8 × 35; 12% of 250 is a quarter of 120.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the approximate value of ?:
√2499.6 × 3.98 + ∛1330.9 ≈ ?

solution.concept: Nearest perfect square and perfect cube
solution.explanation: √2499.6 ≈ √2500 = 50 and 3.98 ≈ 4, so the product is about 200. ∛1330.9 ≈ ∛1331 = 11. 200 + 11 ≈ 211, and the nearest option is 210 (exact 209.98).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value will replace the question mark?
1439.8 ÷ 24.03 + 18.97 × 7.02 ≈ ?

solution.concept: Round each number to a value that divides or multiplies cleanly

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should come in place of the question mark (?)?
?% of 1249.7 + 27.98% of 650.2 ≈ 432.1

solution.concept: Rounding, then solving for the unknown percentage

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the approximate value of ?:
√(1155.8 + √4223.9) ≈ ?

solution.concept: Approximate the inner root first, then the outer one

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should replace ? in the expression
5/8 of 1279.6 + 3/7 of 841.2 − 19.98² ≈ ?

solution.concept: Round to multiples of the fraction's denominator

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should come in place of the question mark (?)?
(12.98 × 15.03 − 44.99) ÷ 6.02 ≈ ?

solution.concept: Round to whole numbers and keep the bracket together

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the approximate value of ?:
∛2196.8 × 6.98 + 39.96% of 1149.8 ≈ ?

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should come in place of the question mark (?)?
2047.9 ÷ ? + 24.02 × 4.98 ≈ 247.1

solution.concept: Unknown in the denominator: isolate the quotient first

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should come in place of the question mark (?)?
(44.98% of 1599.7 + √3135.9) ÷ 7.98 ≈ ? − 13.97²

solution.concept: Multi-term approximation with the unknown on the right side
solution.why_others_wrong: 286 leaves out √3135.9 (720 ÷ 8 + 196); 313 and 273 are 20 away from the computed value.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the approximate value of ?:
?² − 36.02% of 1249.8 + ∛3374.7 × 8.97 ≈ 1285.2

solution.concept: Cube root and percentage approximation, then solving for ?²
solution.why_others_wrong: 35, 45 and 50 square to 1,225, 2,025 and 2,500, far from 1,600.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should replace ? in
(17.02² − 12.98²) × 4.99 ÷ 9.97 + 63.01% of 499.8 ≈ ?

solution.concept: Difference of squares a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b) after rounding
solution.shortcut: (a + b)(a − b) avoids squaring 17 and 13 separately.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the series?
11, 13, 16, 21, 28, 39, ?

solution.explanation: The differences are 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, the prime numbers in order. The next prime is 13, so the next term is 39 + 13 = 52.
solution.why_others_wrong: 50 repeats the difference 11; 51 uses 12, which is not prime.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Find the next term of the series: 120, 99, 80, 63, 48, ?

solution.concept: One less than perfect squares, in descending order
solution.shortcut: The differences 21, 19, 17, 15 fall by 2, so the next difference is 13: 48 − 13 = 35.
solution.why_others_wrong: 36 is 6² without the −1; 33 repeats the difference 15.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Which number should replace the question mark?
4, 10, 28, 82, 244, ?

solution.explanation: Each term is three times the previous term minus 2: 4 × 3 − 2 = 10, 10 × 3 − 2 = 28, and so on. The next term is 244 × 3 − 2 = 730.
solution.shortcut: The differences 6, 18, 54, 162 triple, so the next difference is 486: 244 + 486 = 730.
solution.why_others_wrong: 732 multiplies by 3 without subtracting 2; 734 adds 2 instead.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Find the missing number (?) in the series: 64, 96, 144, ?, 324, 486

solution.concept: Each term is 1.5 times the previous term
solution.why_others_wrong: 192 repeats the difference 48; 240 adds 96. Neither continues to 324.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Find the missing term: 7, 8, 10, 14, 22, ?, 70

solution.explanation: The differences are 1, 2, 4, 8, so the next ones are 16 and 32. The missing term is 22 + 16 = 38, and 38 + 32 = 70 confirms it.
solution.why_others_wrong: 30 repeats the difference 8; 46 doubles 22 and adds 2, but 46 → 70 is a difference of 24, not 32.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What will come in place of ? in the series 6, 24, 60, 120, 210, ?

solution.concept: n³ − n, i.e. the product of three consecutive numbers (n − 1) n (n + 1)
solution.why_others_wrong: 343 is 7³ without subtracting 7; 330 adds 120 (repeating a second difference of 30 instead of 36).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What should come in place of the question mark?
11, 25, 47, 97, 191, ?

solution.why_others_wrong: 379 applies −3 twice in a row; 382 doubles without the +3.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Find the next term of the series: 3, 7, 13, 23, 41, 75, ?

solution.concept: Two levels of differences: the second differences double
solution.explanation: First differences: 4, 6, 10, 18, 34. Second differences: 2, 4, 8, 16, which double, so the next is 32. The next first difference is 34 + 32 = 66 and the next term is 75 + 66 = 141.
solution.shortcut: Each difference is twice the previous one minus 2 (6 = 2 × 4 − 2, 10 = 2 × 6 − 2, …): 2 × 34 − 2 = 66.
solution.why_others_wrong: 109 repeats the difference 34; 143 and 147 use second differences of 34 and 38.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?)?
2, 12, 36, 80, 150, 252, ?

solution.shortcut: Check with differences: 10, 24, 44, 70, 102 → second differences 14, 20, 26, 32 → next 38 → 252 + 140 = 392.
solution.why_others_wrong: 343 is 7³ without the 7²; 384 uses a second difference of 30 instead of 38; 400 is 20².

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Which number will replace the question mark?
2, 5, 13, 36, 104, ?

solution.why_others_wrong: 312 multiplies by 3 without subtracting; 308 repeats −4.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Find the missing number: 5, 12, 10, 36, 20, 108, ?, 324

solution.explanation: The terms in odd positions are 5, 10, 20, ? (each doubled) and those in even positions are 12, 36, 108, 324 (each tripled). So the missing term is 20 × 2 = 40.
solution.why_others_wrong: 216 doubles 108 as if the series were one chain; 60 triples 20, mixing the two rules; 30 adds 10.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the wrong number in the series:
2, 6, 18, 54, 160, 486, 1,458

solution.concept: Each term is 3 times the previous term
solution.why_others_wrong: 486 looks wrong if you divide by 160, but it equals 3 × 162.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Which number in the series below does not fit the pattern?
7, 16, 35, 72, 153, 312, 631

solution.explanation: The rule is ×2 + 2, ×2 + 3, ×2 + 4, ×2 + 5, … The fourth term should be 35 × 2 + 4 = 74, and 74 × 2 + 5 = 153 confirms that 72 is wrong.
solution.why_others_wrong: 153 looks wrong if you continue from 72 (72 × 2 + 5 = 149), but it fits the correct value 74.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the wrong number in the series:
1, 2, 6, 21, 88, 446, 2,676

solution.concept: Multiply by n and add n: ×1 + 1, ×2 + 2, ×3 + 3, …
solution.why_others_wrong: 2,676 looks wrong if you continue from 446 (446 × 6 + 6 = 2,682), but it fits 445.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Exactly one term of this series is incorrect. Which one?
4, 3, 5, 15, 55, 274, 1,643

solution.concept: Multiply by 1, 2, 3, … and subtract 1 each time
solution.why_others_wrong: 55 looks wrong if you continue from 15 (15 × 4 − 1 = 59), but it fits the correct value 14.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
In the following question, two equations I and II are given. Solve both and choose the correct relation between x and y.
I. x² − 15x + 56 = 0
II. y² − 3y − 10 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Factorising by splitting the middle term; a negative constant term gives roots of opposite signs
solution.explanation: x = 7 or 8. y = 5 or −2. The smallest x (7) is greater than the largest y (5), so x > y.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the roots of both equations below and state how x and y are related.
I. x² + 3x − 40 = 0
II. y² − 2y − 15 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Compare every pair of roots; a shared root plus opposite-side roots means no relation holds
solution.explanation: x = 5 or −8 and y = 5 or −3. x = −8 is smaller than both values of y, but x = 5 is greater than y = −3. So no single relation holds.
solution.why_others_wrong: x ≥ y and x ≤ y come from noticing the common root 5 and checking only one other pair.
solution.final_answer: Option B: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Compare the roots of the following pair of equations and choose the relation between x and y that is always true.
I. 3x² − 19x + 30 = 0
II. 4y² − 25y + 36 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: When the root ranges overlap, no single relation holds
solution.explanation: x = 3 or 3.33 and y = 4 or 2.25. x is less than y = 4 but greater than y = 2.25, so no relation holds.
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y comes from comparing only the larger roots (3.33 and 4).
solution.final_answer: Option C: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Work out every possible value of x and of y, then pick the relation that always holds.
I. x² = 289
II. y = √289

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: x² = k gives x = ±√k, but the symbol √k means only the positive root
solution.explanation: x² = 289 gives x = 17 or −17. y = √289 is the principal (positive) square root, so y = 17 only. x is either equal to y or smaller, so x ≤ y.
steps: II: y = +17 (the radical sign denotes the non-negative root)
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y misses the case x = y = 17; x ≥ y treats y = √289 as ±17 as well.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
One equation is linear and the other quadratic. Solve both and choose the correct relationship.
I. 4x − 7 = 2x + 9
II. y² − 17y + 72 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Solve the linear equation directly; factorise the quadratic
solution.explanation: I: 2x = 16, so x = 8. II: (y − 8)(y − 9) = 0, so y = 8 or 9. x is equal to or smaller than y, so x ≤ y.
steps: x = 8 = y (when y = 8) and x < y (when y = 9)
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y ignores y = 8.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
In the question below, solve equations I and II and identify the correct relation between x and y.
I. x² − (√3 + √2)x + √6 = 0
II. y² − 3√3y + 6 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Quadratics with surd coefficients: find two roots from their sum and product
solution.explanation: For I, the roots have sum √3 + √2 and product √6, so x = √3 or √2. For II, the roots have sum 3√3 and product 6, so y = √3 or 2√3. The largest x (√3) equals the smallest y (√3), so x ≤ y.
solution.shortcut: All roots are positive, so compare squares: x² ∈ {3, 2}, y² ∈ {3, 12}.
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y misses the shared root √3.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Solve both equations and choose the option that correctly relates x and y.
I. 6x² + 13x + 6 = 0
II. 6y² + 5y − 6 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Factorising with a ≠ 1; check all four pairs
solution.explanation: x = −1.5 or −0.67 and y = −1.5 or 0.67. x = −0.67 is greater than y = −1.5 but less than y = 0.67, so no relation holds.
solution.why_others_wrong: x ≤ y comes from checking only x = −1.5 against both values of y.
solution.final_answer: Option B: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find all real values of x and y and choose the correct relation.
I. x³ − 512 = 0
II. y² − 15y + 56 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: A cube equation x³ = k has exactly one real root
solution.explanation: x³ = 512 has the single real root x = 8. y = 7 or 8. So x is greater than or equal to y: x ≥ y.
steps: I: x³ = 512 = 8³ ⇒ x = 8 (the only real root)
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y misses y = 8; x ≤ y comes from treating x³ = 512 like a square and adding x = −8.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Solve both equations and choose the correct relation between x and y.
I. 2x² + 15x + 28 = 0
II. 5y² + 13y + 6 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: All coefficients positive ⇒ both roots negative; compare carefully on the negative side
solution.explanation: x = −3.5 or −4 and y = −0.6 or −2. The largest x (−3.5) is less than the smallest y (−2), so x < y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y comes from comparing the sizes 3.5, 4 with 0.6, 2 and forgetting the negative signs.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If the six-digit number 473x28 is divisible by 11, what is the digit x?

solution.concept: Divisibility by 11: (sum of digits in odd places) − (sum of digits in even places) must be 0 or a multiple of 11
solution.explanation: From the left, the odd places hold 4, 3, 2 (sum 9) and the even places hold 7, x, 8 (sum 15 + x). The difference 9 − (15 + x) = −(6 + x) must be a multiple of 11, so 6 + x = 11 and x = 5.
solution.why_others_wrong: 6, 4 and 7 make the difference −12, −10 and −13, none of which is a multiple of 11.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Two numbers are in the ratio 4 : 7 and their LCM is 1,092. What is the sum of the two numbers?

solution.concept: Numbers in ratio a : b (co-prime) are ak and bk with HCF k and LCM abk
solution.explanation: Let the numbers be 4k and 7k. Since 4 and 7 are co-prime, the LCM is 28k = 1,092, so k = 39. The numbers are 156 and 273, and their sum is 429.
solution.why_others_wrong: 273 is only the larger number; 546 is half the LCM, not the sum of the numbers; 390 would need k = 35, but 1,092 ÷ 28 = 39.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the remainder when 2¹⁰⁰ is divided by 7?

solution.concept: Find a power of the base that leaves remainder 1, then reduce the exponent
solution.explanation: 2³ = 8 leaves remainder 1 on division by 7. 2¹⁰⁰ = (2³)³³ × 2¹, so the remainder is 1³³ × 2 = 2.
solution.shortcut: Remainders of 2ⁿ ÷ 7 cycle 2, 4, 1; 100 leaves remainder 1 on division by 3, so take the first value, 2.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1 assumes 100 is a multiple of 3; 4 picks the second value of the cycle (as for an exponent ≡ 2 mod 3).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many zeros are there at the end of 250! (the product 1 × 2 × 3 × … × 250)?

solution.concept: Trailing zeros = number of factors 5 in n! (factors of 2 are always more): ⌊n/5⌋ + ⌊n/25⌋ + ⌊n/125⌋ + …
solution.explanation: Each trailing zero needs one factor 10 = 2 × 5, and 5s are scarcer than 2s. Multiples of 5 up to 250 give 50 fives, multiples of 25 give 10 extra, and multiples of 125 give 2 more. Total = 62.
solution.why_others_wrong: 50 counts each multiple of 5 once; 60 stops at 25 and misses 125 and 250 (5³ factors); 52 skips the multiples of 25.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In an examination a candidate needs 40% of the maximum marks to pass. She scores 288 marks and fails by 12 marks. What are the maximum marks?

solution.concept: Pass marks = marks scored + shortfall = 40% of maximum
solution.explanation: The pass mark is 288 + 12 = 300. 300 is 40% of the maximum, so the maximum = 300 ÷ 0.4 = 750.
solution.why_others_wrong: 720 treats 288 as the pass mark; 690 subtracts 12 instead of adding it.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The price of cooking oil rises by 25%. By what percentage must a household cut its consumption so that its spending on oil does not change?

solution.concept: Spending = price × consumption; reduction needed = r ÷ (100 + r) × 100
solution.explanation: If the price becomes 125/100 of the old price, consumption must become 100/125 = 4/5 of the old amount, a cut of 1/5 = 20%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 25% simply copies the price rise; 16⅔% is the cut needed for a 20% price rise.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Rohit spends 72% of his monthly income and saves the rest. If he saves ₹7,840 a month, what is his monthly income?

solution.explanation: He saves 100 − 72 = 28% of his income. 28% of income = ₹7,840, so income = 7,840 ÷ 0.28 = ₹28,000.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹20,160 is his expenditure (72% of ₹28,000); ₹10,889 divides 7,840 by 0.72.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A town has 50,000 people. Every year its population grows by a birth rate of 3.2% and falls by a death rate of 1.2% of the population at the start of that year (ignore migration). What will the population be after 2 years?

solution.concept: Net growth rate = birth rate − death rate, compounded yearly
solution.explanation: The net growth is 3.2% − 1.2% = 2% a year, compounded. After 2 years the population is 50,000 × 1.02 × 1.02 = 52,020.
solution.why_others_wrong: 52,000 adds 2% twice on the original population (no compounding); 48,020 treats the net rate as a 2% fall.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Two numbers are 20% and 50% more than a third number respectively. What percentage of the second number is the first number?

solution.concept: Take the third number as 100 to compare the other two
solution.explanation: If the third number is 100, the first is 120 and the second is 150. 120 ÷ 150 × 100 = 80%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 70% subtracts the percentages (100 − 30); 125% is the second number as a percentage of the first.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Sunita's income rises by 20% and her expenditure rises by 12%. As a result her savings rise by 32%. What percentage of her original income did she originally spend?

solution.concept: Income = expenditure + savings, before and after the change
solution.explanation: Take income = 100 and expenditure = E, so savings = 100 − E. After the change, income = 120, expenditure = 1.12E and savings = 1.32(100 − E). So 120 − 1.12E = 132 − 1.32E, giving 0.2E = 12 and E = 60. She spent 60% of her income.
solution.why_others_wrong: 40% is the savings share, not the spending share; 66⅔% and 50% fail the check (savings would change by 36% and 28%).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If A : B = 3 : 4 and B : C = 6 : 7, what is A : B : C?

solution.concept: Make the common term (B) equal in both ratios
solution.explanation: B is 4 in the first ratio and 6 in the second. Make both 12: A : B = 9 : 12 and B : C = 12 : 14. So A : B : C = 9 : 12 : 14.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3 : 4 : 7 joins the ratios without matching B; 9 : 12 : 7 scales only the first ratio; 6 : 8 : 7 scales the first ratio by 2 but not the second.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What number must be subtracted from each of 23, 30, 57 and 78 so that the four results are in proportion?

solution.concept: a : b = c : d means a × d = b × c (product of extremes = product of means)
solution.explanation: Let x be subtracted. Then (23 − x)(78 − x) = (30 − x)(57 − x). Expanding, 1794 − 101x + x² = 1710 − 87x + x², so 84 = 14x and x = 6. The numbers become 17, 24, 51, 72, and 17 : 24 = 51 : 72.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4, 5 and 7 fail the check: for example 19 × 74 = 1406 but 26 × 53 = 1378.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: ₹3,800 is divided among A, B and C so that 4 times A's share, 6 times B's share and 9 times C's share are all equal. What is C's share?

solution.explanation: Let 4A = 6B = 9C = k. Then A : B : C = k/4 : k/6 : k/9 = 9 : 6 : 4 (multiplying by 36). C gets 4/19 of ₹3,800 = ₹800.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹1,800 uses the ratio 4 : 6 : 9 directly instead of the reciprocals; ₹1,200 is B's share.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The present ages of a father and his son are in the ratio 7 : 2, and the product of their ages is 896. What will be the ratio of their ages 6 years from now?

solution.concept: Write the ages as 7k and 2k and use the product to find k
solution.explanation: 7k × 2k = 14k² = 896, so k² = 64 and k = 8. The father is 56 and the son 16. In 6 years they will be 62 and 22, a ratio of 31 : 11.
solution.why_others_wrong: 7 : 2 is the present ratio (a ratio of ages changes with time); 8 : 3 is the ratio after 8 years and 3 : 1 after 4 years.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Two numbers are in the ratio 3 : 5. If 9 is subtracted from each, the ratio becomes 12 : 23. What is the smaller number?

solution.concept: Set up one equation in the common multiplier k
solution.explanation: Let the numbers be 3k and 5k. (3k − 9)/(5k − 9) = 12/23 gives 69k − 207 = 60k − 108, so 9k = 99 and k = 11. The smaller number is 33.
solution.why_others_wrong: 55 is the larger number; 27 and 36 fail the check (18 : 36 and 27 : 51 are not 12 : 23).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The sum of the ages of five children born at intervals of 3 years each is 50 years. What is the age of the youngest child?

solution.concept: Ages in arithmetic progression: y, y + 3, y + 6, y + 9, y + 12
solution.explanation: The ages are y, y + 3, y + 6, y + 9 and y + 12, with sum 5y + 30 = 50. So 5y = 20 and y = 4.
solution.why_others_wrong: 10 years is the average (the middle child); 16 years is the eldest.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A is now twice as old as B was when A was as old as B is now. If A is 40 years old now, how old is B now?

solution.concept: Translate each clause; the age gap between two people never changes
solution.explanation: Let B be b years old now. A was b years old 40 − b years ago, and B was then b − (40 − b) = 2b − 40. A's present age is twice that: 40 = 2(2b − 40), so 4b = 120 and b = 30.
steps: A was b years old (40 − b) years ago
Check: 10 years ago A was 30 (B's age now) and B was 20; 40 = 2 × 20
solution.why_others_wrong: 20 years is B's age at that earlier time, not now.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Five years ago, Neha's age was the square of her son's age at that time. Four years from now, Neha will be three times as old as her son. What is Neha's present age?

solution.concept: Let the son's age five years ago be a; Neha's was a². Form a quadratic and keep the positive root
solution.explanation: Now Neha is a² + 5 and her son a + 5. In four years: a² + 9 = 3(a + 9), so a² − 3a − 18 = 0, i.e. (a − 6)(a + 3) = 0 and a = 6. Neha's present age = 36 + 5 = 41.
steps: Five years ago: son a, Neha a²
In 4 years: son a + 9, Neha a² + 9
solution.why_others_wrong: 36 years is her age five years ago; 45 years is her age four years from now; 11 years is the son's present age.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The average of five numbers is 48. When one number is removed, the average of the remaining four is 45. Which number was removed?

solution.explanation: Total of five = 5 × 48 = 240. Total of four = 4 × 45 = 180. The removed number is 240 − 180 = 60.
solution.shortcut: The removed number is 48 + 4 × 3 = 60: it is above the old average by 3 for each of the 4 that remain.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3 is only the drop in the average; 51 adds 3 to 48 once instead of four times.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A batsman has an average of 42 runs over 16 innings. How many runs must he score in the 17th innings to raise his average to 45?

solution.concept: New total − old total = runs needed in the new innings
solution.explanation: Old total = 16 × 42 = 672. New total needed = 17 × 45 = 765. Runs needed = 765 − 672 = 93.
solution.shortcut: He must score the new average plus 3 for each of the 16 old innings: 45 + 48 = 93.
solution.why_others_wrong: 90 adds 3 × 16 to the old average 42 instead of the new average 45; 45 is the new average itself.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In an office, the 10 officers earn an average of ₹40,000 a month and the other staff earn an average of ₹10,000. The average salary of all employees is ₹15,000. How many other staff are there?

solution.concept: Weighted average: deviations above and below the overall average balance out
solution.explanation: Officers are ₹25,000 above the overall average: 10 × 25,000 = 2,50,000. Each other employee is ₹5,000 below, so their number is 2,50,000 ÷ 5,000 = 50.
solution.shortcut: Alligation: officers : others = (15 − 10) : (40 − 15) = 5 : 25 = 1 : 5, so others = 50.
solution.why_others_wrong: 30, 40 and 60 give overall averages of ₹17,500, ₹16,000 and about ₹14,286.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The average age of 8 men rises by 2 years when two of them, aged 21 and 23, are replaced by two women. What is the average age of the two women?

solution.concept: Replacement: increase in total = number of people × increase in average
solution.explanation: The total age rises by 8 × 2 = 16 years. So the women together are 21 + 23 + 16 = 60 years old, an average of 30 years.
solution.why_others_wrong: 23 adds only 2 years to the total; 24 adds 2 to the men's average 22; 38 gives all 16 years to each woman.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The average of 11 results is 50. The average of the first six is 49 and the average of the last six is 52. What is the sixth result?

solution.concept: The sixth result is counted in both groups of six
solution.explanation: First six total = 294 and last six total = 312. Together they count all 11 results plus the sixth one again, so the sixth = 294 + 312 − 550 = 56.
solution.why_others_wrong: 50.5 averages 49 and 52; 46 subtracts the wrong way (550 − 504).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Sections A, B and C have average marks of 70, 60 and 55. The combined average of A and B is 66, and the combined average of B and C is 57. What is the average mark of all three sections together?

solution.concept: Use each combined average to find the ratio of section sizes, then take the weighted average
solution.explanation: A and B: 70a + 60b = 66(a + b) gives 4a = 6b, so a : b = 3 : 2. B and C: 60b + 55c = 57(b + c) gives 3b = 2c, so b : c = 2 : 3. Hence a : b : c = 3 : 2 : 3 and the overall average is (210 + 120 + 165) ÷ 8 = 61.875.
solution.why_others_wrong: 61.67 is the simple average of 70, 60 and 55, which ignores the different section sizes.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The average of 25 observations was found to be 36. Later it was noticed that the observation 48 had been recorded as 84 and the observation 25 had been recorded as 52. What is the correct average?

solution.concept: Correct total = wrong total − wrong values + right values
solution.explanation: Wrong total = 25 × 36 = 900. Remove the wrong entries 84 and 52 and add the right ones 48 and 25: 900 − 84 − 52 + 48 + 25 = 837. Correct average = 837 ÷ 25 = 33.48.
solution.why_others_wrong: 34.56 corrects only the first error; 35.64 corrects the first error but adds the second excess instead of removing it.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: By selling 33 metres of cloth, a shopkeeper gains the selling price of 11 metres. What is his gain percentage?

solution.concept: Gain = SP − CP; express both in terms of the selling price of one metre
solution.explanation: SP of 33 m − CP of 33 m = SP of 11 m, so CP of 33 m = SP of 22 m. The gain is the SP of 11 m on a cost equal to the SP of 22 m: 11/22 = 50%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 33⅓% takes the gain as a percentage of the selling price (11/33) instead of the cost.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: An article costing ₹800 is marked 35% above its cost price and sold for ₹972. What discount percentage was allowed?

solution.concept: Discount % is always calculated on the marked price
solution.explanation: Marked price = 800 × 1.35 = ₹1,080. Discount = 1,080 − 972 = ₹108, which is 108 ÷ 1,080 = 10% of the marked price.
solution.why_others_wrong: 11.11% divides the discount by the selling price; 21.5% is the profit percentage (172 on 800).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A shopkeeper uses a weight that reads 1 kg but actually holds 1.1 kg when he buys goods, and a weight that reads 1 kg but holds only 900 g when he sells. He buys and sells at the same price per 'kg'. What is his gain percentage?

solution.concept: Compare the quantity he actually receives with the quantity he actually gives for the same money
solution.explanation: For the price of 1 kg he receives 1,100 g when buying and hands over only 900 g when selling. So the money he gets for 900 g would buy him 1,100 g: gain = 1,100/900 − 1 = 2/9 = 22 2/9%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20% adds the two 10% cheats; 21% treats them as successive 10% gains (1.1 × 1.1); 11 1/9% counts only the selling cheat.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A sells a bicycle to B at a profit of 25%, and B sells it to C at a profit of 20%. C pays ₹2,250 more than A's cost price. What was A's cost price?

solution.explanation: C pays 1.25 × 1.20 = 1.5 times A's cost, i.e. 50% more. So 50% of A's cost = ₹2,250 and A's cost = ₹4,500.
steps: C's price = A's cost × 1.25 × 1.20 = 1.5 × A's cost
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹5,000 adds the profit percentages (25 + 20 = 45%); ₹6,750 is what C paid.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A dealer sold two mobile phones for ₹2,400 each. On one he gained 20% and on the other he lost 20%. What is his overall gain or loss percentage?

solution.concept: Equal selling prices with equal gain and loss % always give a net loss of (x/10)² %
